items.prompt: Priya's director confirmed the merge itself is happening, but HR hasn't finalized which 5 roles are cut. What should Priya tell her team about these two facts?
choices: Say only that 'some changes may be coming' and leave both facts vague until everything is final
State plainly that the merge is decided, and separately and just as plainly that which roles are affected is not decided yet
Withhold the merge news entirely until the role list is also final, so she only has to say it once
Tell the team the merge is 'probably' happening, to soften it in case it falls through
items.explanation: Blurring a locked fact and an open one into one vague statement makes even the settled part sound uncertain. Naming each plainly — this part is decided, this part isn't — gives the team the most accurate picture available.
items.reference:
Decided

The merge is happening: 15 → 10

Not decided

Which 5 roles, until HR finalizes it

Why: naming both halves plainly stops the whole situation from reading as one giant unknown.
items.learnMore:
Splitting known from unknown

A change is rarely 100% decided or 0% decided — usually part of it is locked while another part is genuinely still open. Blurring the two into one vague 'some changes are coming' makes even the settled part sound uncertain, which is worse than it needs to be.

Priya's merge is a clean example: the merge itself is locked at the director level. Who ends up in which of the 10 remaining seats is not. Saying both sentences, plainly, in that order, gives the team the most accurate picture available — not the most comfortable one, the most accurate one.

Common mistake

Treating 'I don't have all the details yet' as equivalent to 'nothing is decided.' Often something real is locked in even when the personal-impact details aren't — say the locked part.

items.prompt: Dev asks Priya 'is my job safe?' before HR has finalized anything. Priya doesn't actually know. What should she avoid saying?
choices: Avoid answering the question at all, and change the subject
Avoid saying 'don't worry, you're safe' — a reassurance she has no standing to guarantee yet
Avoid mentioning that a decision process is even underway
Avoid using the word 'layoff' under any circumstances
items.explanation: A reassurance made without the information to back it up is a promise, not a comfort. If it turns out false, the damage isn't just the bad news later — it's that Priya's word stopped being reliable on exactly the topic that matters most.
items.reference:
🤞 "Don't worry, you're safe" — a promise with no standing behind it
✅ "I don't know yet, and I won't pretend I do" — honest, still useful

Why: a broken reassurance costs more trust than the original bad news would have on its own.
items.learnMore:
Why false reassurance costs more than honest uncertainty

A reassurance made without the standing to guarantee it (Priya doesn't have the list yet) is a promise, not a comfort. If it turns out true, nothing is gained beyond what honest uncertainty would have given anyway. If it turns out false, the person hearing it now has two losses instead of one: the role, and the discovery that their manager's word doesn't reliably mean anything.

Every future hard conversation with that person, and often with the rest of the team who hears about it, now carries a discount — 'reassuring' stops functioning as information.

Common mistake

Believing a comforting lie is kinder in the moment. It's kinder in the moment and much more expensive later, exactly when trust matters most.

items.prompt: Which is the better thing for Priya to tell her team about when they'll hear more?
choices: "I'll let you know as soon as I know something"
"I'll have real names by Friday the 12th, and I'll tell you that day, whatever it is"
"Try not to think about it until HR is fully done"
"I can't give any kind of timeline"
items.explanation: A specific date turns an open-ended wait into a bounded one, which is measurably easier to sit with — and it creates a commitment the team can hold Priya to, rather than an indefinite promise that could stretch on without anyone noticing.
items.reference:
"Soon"open-ended, no end point
"Friday the 12th"bounded, a specific date

Why: a bounded wait is measurably easier to sit with than an open-ended one, even when the news at the end is the same.
items.learnMore:
Why a concrete date matters more than it seems

'Soon' and 'as soon as I know' both sound reassuring but give the listener nothing to plan against — every day that passes without news can just as easily mean 'still not decided' as 'decided but not yet told.' A specific date collapses that ambiguity: before the date, there's genuinely nothing to report; after it, there's news either way.

The date also creates accountability for the manager — missing a promised check-in is its own trust cost, which is exactly why Priya sends a short 'nothing new yet, still on track' update partway through rather than letting the date arrive as the first sign of life.

Common mistake

Setting a date and then letting it quietly slip without comment. A missed, unacknowledged check-in is often worse than never having promised one.

It's weaker only because it sounds less formal

items.explanation: Without a bound, every quiet day could mean either 'nothing to report yet' or 'something happened and hasn't been shared.' A calendar date removes that ambiguity entirely — before it, there's nothing to report; at it, there's news either way.

items.prompt: Priya could deliver only the organizational facts (the merge, the new team size) and never mention personal impact at all. Why is that a mistake, even though it's technically all true?
choices: It isn't a mistake — personal impact should never be discussed in a group setting
Everyone in the room is already privately wondering 'what does this mean for me,' and leaving it unaddressed doesn't remove the question, it just means no one hears an honest answer to it
It's a mistake only if someone directly asks about their own role
Personal impact only matters for the people who end up affected
items.explanation: The personal-impact question exists in everyone's head regardless of whether it's spoken. Naming it out loud, even without a full answer, replaces silent worst-case guessing with an honest partial answer.
items.reference:
🤐 Question left unspoken → people assume the worst answer silently
🗣️ Question named out loud → answered honestly, even if incomplete

Why: everyone is privately asking 'what does this mean for me' — naming it beats hoping no one asks.
items.learnMore:
Naming the question people are already asking

Every person hearing disruptive organizational news is running the same private calculation, whether or not they say it aloud: what does this actually mean for me, specifically? Leaving that question unaddressed doesn't make it go away — it just means each person answers it silently, usually with the worst plausible version, and the manager never gets the chance to correct it.

Naming it out loud — 'I know the question on everyone's mind is what this means for your role' — doesn't require having a full answer. It requires acknowledging the question exists and giving whatever honest partial answer is available.

Common mistake

Assuming that not bringing up personal impact spares people from worrying about it. It doesn't — it just means they worry about it without ever hearing the manager's honest, partial answer.

items.prompt: What's the risk of Priya announcing the merge to her team before her director has actually finalized it at the leadership level?
choices: There's no risk — earlier is always better
If the plan changes after being announced as fact, the team learns that 'confirmed' from Priya doesn't always mean confirmed, which costs credibility on future announcements
It would violate a law requiring formal HR notice first
The team would simply forget the early announcement by the time anything real happens
items.explanation: Announcing something before it's genuinely decided risks having to walk it back if it changes, which teaches the team not to fully trust the word 'confirmed' the next time — a distinct cost from the cost of staying silent too long.
items.reference:
Too early

Announcing a maybe before it's decided

Too late

Rumor has already filled the gap

Why: timing is a separate decision from wording — good wording delivered at the wrong moment still lands badly.
items.learnMore:
Over-communicating early vs. staying silent too long

Announcing a change before it's actually decided risks teaching the team that 'confirmed' from a manager doesn't always mean confirmed — if the plan changes after being announced, credibility takes the hit even though the manager was acting on the best information available at the time.

Waiting too long has the opposite failure mode: once a signal has already leaked (like Priya's calendar invite), every additional hour of silence is filled by rumor, and the manager ends up correcting a story instead of telling one.

Common mistake

Treating 'communicate early' as always better. It's only better once something is actually decided — announcing a proposal as a fact creates its own, different trust problem.

items.prompt: Priya's team already noticed the calendar invite. If she waits and says nothing until she has full certainty, what does the team do with that gap in the meantime?
choices: They wait patiently and assume nothing significant is happening
They fill it themselves, typically rehearsing the worst plausible version, because an unexplained gap after a visible signal reads as something being hidden
They forget about the calendar invite entirely within a day or two
They wait for HR to make an official announcement instead
items.explanation: A team doesn't sit neutrally with an unexplained gap — especially after already noticing a signal. They tend to assume the worst plausible version, because silence after a visible sign of change reads as something being actively hidden.
items.reference:
🤐 Silence → team fills the gap with the worst plausible version
🗣️ Named uncertainty → team has a confirmed, bounded fact instead

Why: a silent gap in information reads as something being hidden, which is scarier than most specific facts.
items.learnMore:
Why silence is read as evidence, not neutrality

When a team notices a signal (a calendar invite, a closed door, a canceled meeting) and then hears nothing from their manager, they don't default to 'probably nothing.' An unexplained gap in information reads as something being actively withheld, and people tend to rehearse the worst plausible version rather than sit neutrally with not knowing.

Acknowledging the change — even without full details — replaces that vacuum with a confirmed, bounded fact the manager can actually be held to, which is a meaningfully different experience than an unconfirmed rumor with no source to check it against.

Common mistake

Assuming that saying nothing is neutral. In practice, silence after a visible signal actively fuels the worst version of the story, it doesn't prevent one.

items.prompt: Compare two managers: one says 'I don't know yet' and it turns out badly for the employee; another says 'don't worry, you're fine' and it also turns out badly. What's the actual difference in cost between the two?
choices: No difference — the employee loses their role either way
The second manager's employee absorbs two losses instead of one: the role, plus the discovery that the manager's reassurance couldn't be trusted
The first manager's approach is worse because it offered no comfort at all
There's no way to know which approach costs more
items.explanation: The bad outcome is identical either way. What differs is whether the manager's word also takes damage — a broken reassurance is a second, separate loss on top of the original news, one that honest uncertainty never creates.
items.reference:
Honest uncertainty, later confirmed bad

One loss: the role

False reassurance, later contradicted

Two losses: the role, and trust in the manager's word

Why: a broken promise compounds bad news instead of just preceding it.
items.learnMore:
The compounding cost of a broken reassurance

The bad news itself — a role being eliminated — is the same regardless of what the manager said beforehand. What a false reassurance adds is a second, separate loss: the discovery that the manager's word, on exactly this topic, wasn't reliable. That second loss doesn't stay contained to this one conversation — it discounts every future 'don't worry' the same manager offers.

Honest uncertainty ('I don't know yet') never creates that second loss, because it never made a claim that could later be proven false. The discomfort of not knowing is real, but it's a single, contained cost rather than a compounding one.

Common mistake

Measuring a reassurance's cost only by whether it turns out true. Even a reassurance that happens to be right doesn't add trust beyond what honest uncertainty would have — it just avoids the downside.

items.prompt: A change is decided at the leadership level, but no one on the team has noticed anything yet. What's the right timing, per the timing tree?

Tell them soon, proactively, on the manager's own terms — hearing it first from the manager is what keeps the manager the trusted source

items.learnMore:
Timing is its own decision, separate from wording

Getting the four moves' wording exactly right doesn't help if the timing is wrong — announcing a still-open proposal as settled fact, or sitting on decided-and-leaked news, both cause damage regardless of how well-crafted the words are.

The tree has three branches: still just a proposal (wait), decided but no signal has leaked yet (tell them soon, proactively, on your own terms), and decided with a signal already leaked (tell them today, because the gap is already being filled). Priya's situation is the third branch specifically because both conditions — decided, and already leaked — are true at once.

Treating 'communicate early' as a universal rule rather than reading which branch of the tree the actual situation sits on. The right timing depends on both whether it's decided and whether it's leaked.

items.prompt: Priya tells Sam about the layoff privately, before running the group meeting with the rest of the team. Why not just announce the final list to everyone at once?

Group announcements are against company policy

items.explanation: Announcing to the group first would mean Sam finds out at the same moment as colleagues, with no room to react privately, and it flattens the most consequential individual news into one line of a structural update rather than a real conversation.

👥 Group meeting: structural news and support details, after

Why: a specific, individually consequential loss deserves privacy and room to react, not a shared line item in a group readout.
items.learnMore:
Why the hardest individual news goes first, and privately

Learning you've lost your role in the same moment as everyone else, in a group setting, with no privacy to react, compounds the loss itself with a lack of dignity in how it was delivered. It also flattens what is, for that person, the single most consequential piece of news into one line of an org-chart update.

Telling Sam privately, before the group meeting, gives them room to actually react and ask questions, and it means Priya is talking with them rather than at them — while the group meeting afterward can focus on structural facts and support without anyone in the room learning their own fate live in front of colleagues.

Common mistake

Folding an individual layoff notification into a group announcement for efficiency. It saves the manager one conversation at the direct cost of the affected person's dignity and privacy.

items.learnMore:
What changes, and what doesn't, at larger scale or worse news

What changes at scale is the mechanism for individual follow-up: a private 1:1 with all 40 people in a department in one afternoon isn't realistic the way it was with 8.

The content of the message doesn't need to shrink — the delivery format does need rethinking (smaller group breakouts led by direct managers, a written FAQ that still names the personal-impact question directly, staggered individual check-ins over days instead of hours) so people still get something more personal than a single mass communication.

items.explanation: With full dissolution, there's no personal variation left to acknowledge — everyone has the same answer, known immediately, which changes the move from managing an open question to communicating a shared, certain outcome as directly and early as possible.
items.reference:
👥 8-person team → individual 1:1s are feasible in an afternoon
🏢 40-person department → the same format doesn't scale the same way

Why: the four moves still apply at scale — the follow-up format has to change to still deliver them.
items.learnMore:
What changes, and what doesn't, at larger scale or worse news

The four moves — known vs. unknown, no false reassurance, a concrete date, naming the personal-impact question — are not specific to an 8-person team. What changes at scale is the mechanism for individual follow-up: a private 1:1 with all 40 people in a department in one afternoon isn't realistic the way it was with 8.

The content of the message doesn't need to shrink — the delivery format does need rethinking (smaller group breakouts led by direct managers, a written FAQ that still names the personal-impact question directly, staggered individual check-ins over days instead of hours) so people still get something more personal than a single mass communication.
